summary:
Lunar Prime shows when a site on the Moon gets sunlight for power and has Earth in view for direct radio contact. Mission planners need both, and they change from site to site and day to day.

You pick two sites on a 3D globe, or start from real missions such as IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3 and Blue Ghost. Lunar Prime computes where the Sun and Earth sit in each site’s sky using NASA/JPL’s SPICE toolkit and the DE440 ephemeris, including lunar libration. Scrub through time and you see the Sun’s elevation, the countdown to the next sunset or Earthset, the longest night, the longest communication blackout, and a list of every sunlight and Earth-contact window. You can also compare one site on two dates. An Explain mode puts each result into plain language.

Near the south pole the Sun and Earth stay close to the horizon, so a ridge or crater wall can block them. For key polar sites, Lunar Prime uses real skylines built from NASA’s LOLA elevation maps. On the Shackleton crater rim the Sun stays up for the whole month we tested, while the crater floor 11 km away gets no sunlight at all in 2027.
details:
What it does

Lunar Prime shows when a spot on the Moon gets sunlight and when it can see Earth. A lander needs sunlight for power and a direct line to Earth to talk home without a relay. You pick two sites on a 3D globe, or one site on two dates, and Lunar Prime puts them side by side.

How it works

The backend uses NASA/JPL’s SPICE toolkit and the DE440 ephemeris to compute where the Sun and Earth sit in each site’s sky, step by step through the chosen dates. Lunar libration is included, which is why Earth rises and sets at sites near the poles. When the Sun or Earth crosses the horizon, the exact time is found to within one second.

Near the south pole the Sun stays close to the horizon, so a crater wall decides whether a site is lit. For four south-pole sites we built real skylines from NASA’s LOLA 80 m elevation map. In 720 directions around each site, we trace across the terrain and record the highest angle it reaches. The Sun or Earth counts as visible only when it clears that skyline.

The app shows:

  • a one-line answer
  • a metrics table: sunlight time, Earth-contact time, longest night and longest communication blackout
  • sky plots with countdowns to the next sunset or Earthset
  • timelines
  • a list of every sunlight and Earth-contact window

Benefits and impact

Picking a landing site and date means trading power against communication, and near the pole both can change within a few kilometres. On the Shackleton crater rim, the Sun stays up for the whole month we tested, while the crater floor 11 km away gets no sunlight at all in 2027. Lunar Prime makes differences like this visible in seconds. It is built for mission planners, but an Explain mode and tooltips put every number into plain language, so students and the public can use it too.

Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SpiceyPy and Rasterio.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js, React Three Fiber and Plotly.
  • Data: NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440), LRO LOLA south-pole elevation maps, and the NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit for the globe.

On a Mac, one double-click starts the whole app.

What makes it creative

Instead of handing you a single percentage, Lunar Prime lets you watch the sky. You can scrub through time and see the Sun skim along the real ridgeline at Shackleton, or replay the same site on two different dates and see how the answer changes.

What we considered

  • Accuracy first. Every number comes from SPICE, and our elevations match SPICE’s own reference routine to within 0.00003°. The LOLA map gives a height at IM-1’s landing point within 13 m of NASA’s published figure.
  • Clear limits. Sunlight is not the same as power, and Earth in view is not a guaranteed radio link. Terrain is used at the four south-pole sites, while other sites use a smooth Moon.
  • Readability. One accessible font, and colour used only for the Sun (yellow) and Earth (blue).
dataRefs: NASA/JPL NAIF Lunar Orientation and Frame Kernels (DE440)
LRO LOLA South Pole Elevation Maps (NASA GSFC PGDA Product 90)
NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit (LRO LROC color map and LOLA elevation)
